items.title: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions, Zelenskyy condemns it as 'wrong'
items.summary: Trump signed the Graham Bill, which targeted Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, into law in September.
items.content:
Trump waives Russia-linked sanctions, citing national interest
U.S. President Donald Trump invoked the Graham Act’s national-interest waiver to suspend new duties on Russian goods and major Russian energy buyers.
The moves drew praise from a Russian envoy and criticism from Democrats and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The waiver came two days before the law’s implementation deadline and follows a separate temporary easing of sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
U.S. President Donald Trump welcomes Russian President Vladimir Putin to Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on Aug. 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday condemned the White House's waiver of key provisions of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine.
"... The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy said in a post on X . "And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people."
President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving key parts of the new U.S. sanctions on Russia.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States," Trump wrote in Friday's order.
The House passed the Russia sanctions bill on Sept. 16, and Trump signed it into law two days later. The bill was introduced over a year ago, and its primary backer was the late Lindsey Graham , a veteran Republican senator who represented South Carolina.
Titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 , the legislation targeted Russia's economy, intending to penalize the country over its continued full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The act required the president to increase duties on all Russian goods imported into the U.S. by up to 500% no later than 30 days after enactment. It also required Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries including China and India that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas.
Trump's latest order waives these two parts of the Graham Act and comes two days before the law's implementation deadline. However, the order preserves existing sanctions on Russia under earlier executive orders.
Zelenskyy said he expects Trump to waive other sanctions on Russia, too.
"Sanctions relief will continue," he posted on X. "I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately."
The law could also sanction Russian leaders, officials, and financial institutions, and expand sanctions on Iran.
Oil sales revenue is critical to funding Russia's war effort.
The move also comes a week after the Trump administration temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027 to ease a supply crunch caused by the war in Iran.
High fuel prices are a sensitive issue for voters ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
"The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's economy envoy, said in a post on X.
"The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," Dmitriev added.
But Trump's opponents have criticized the move.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who also drafted the Graham Act, condemned the latest waiver.
"Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug & the enablers of Russia's war machine & against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, & our European allies," Blumenthal said in an X post.
BRUSSELS, BELGIUM - OCTOBER 16: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy holds a press conference during the second day of the European Union leaders' summit in Brussels, Belgium, on October 16, 2026. (Photo by Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy had warned that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives.
"Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry."
Earlier this week, reports emerged that Ukraine has restricted SpaceX's  Starlink military application, Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.

items.title: Trump suspends Russia sanctions as deadly attacks plunge Ukraine into darkness - Vatican News
items.summary: Trump suspends Russia sanctions as deadly attacks plunge Ukraine into darkness  Vatican News
items.content:
US President Donald Trump, right, and Russian President Vladimir Putin (AFP or licensors)
Trump suspends Russia sanctions as deadly attacks plunge Ukraine into darkness
Donald Trump suspends recently passed sanctions and tariffs aimed at Russia that were due to take effect in just a few days, prompting criticism from Ukraine and from European allies.
U.S. President Donald Trump has suspended sweeping new sanctions against Russia, citing American national interests, as Russian missile and drone attacks killed at least eight people in Ukraine and left more than a million without electricity.
The decision has raised concerns over Washingtonâs approach to Russiaâs invasion of Ukraine and highlighted growing differences between the United States and the European Union over how to end the war.
Trump waived key Russia-related sanctions and tariffs just days before they were due to take effect under legislation he signed last month.
The measures included penalties against countries purchasing Russian oil and natural gas, intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The U.S. president cited American national interests amid rising energy prices. His decision followed a controversial agreement allowing more Russian diesel onto global markets, a move Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned would help finance Moscowâs military campaign.
Speaking about the impact on ordinary Ukrainians, Zelenskyy said the additional Russian diesel would do little to reduce fuel prices in the United States but would provide Russia with more money to continue its attacks.
He recalled how Ukrainian children had spent nearly five years growing up amid air raid warnings, seeking shelter underground or attending classes online.
âThey didnât have childhood because of one person, because Putin,â Zelenskyy said, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin. âItâs a mistake. Iâm sure this diesel will not help Americans but will help Putin,â he added.
His remarks came as Russian forces continued launching missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
At least eight people were reportedly killed and 60 others injured in Fridayâs attacks, while more than one million people lost electricity. Ukrainian authorities said repair crews subsequently restored power to more than a million people.
The destruction has renewed concerns about the humanitarian consequences of Russiaâs campaign against Ukraineâs energy network, particularly for families, elderly residents and vulnerable communities facing the coming winter.
Against this backdrop, European Union leaders meeting at a summit in Brussels reaffirmed their support for Ukraine and expressed regret over Washingtonâs decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
EU leaders welcomed a new package of sanctions against Moscow and an agreement to release another 6.6 billion euros, approximately $7.5 billion, in military assistance through the European Peace Facility.
However, they stopped short of approving Zelenskyyâs request for an additional 70 billion euros in financial and military assistance for 2027, instead calling for further assessments of Ukraineâs funding needs.
The developments underscored growing differences between Washington and Brussels over the economic pressure needed to bring Moscow to the negotiating table.
As Russiaâs full-scale invasion approaches its fifth anniversary in February, Ukraine faces mounting civilian casualties, widespread infrastructure damage and uncertainty over the global support needed to sustain its defense and secure a lasting peace.

items.summary: Iran says oil tankers struck by mines in Strait of Hormuz  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
IRGC claims two oil tankers hit naval mines in Strait of Hormuz, caught fire
IRNA reported that the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and attempted to use an unauthorized route through the strategic waterway.
Vessels at the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, October 2, 2026.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy claimed on Saturday that two oil tankers had caught fire after hitting naval mines while crossing the Strait of Hormuz , the official Iranian news agency IRNA reported.
State media said both tankers were carrying about 2 million barrels of crude oil.
There was no independent confirmation of the reports.
IRNA reported that the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and attempted to use an unauthorized route through the strategic waterway . The second vessel was left immobilized after striking a mine, it added.
State media earlier reported that the other tanker had also struck a mine while attempting to transit the strait via a route not authorized by Iran .
A view of shipping containers near a docked container ship at the Aqaba Container Terminal (ACT), which has seen increased vessel traffic amid disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, in Aqaba Tuesday, 1st September 2026 (credit: REUTERS/ALAA AL SUKHNI)
Ongoing war disrupts key shipping route, global energy prices
The incidents come amid heightened tensions around the strait, a key oil shipping route. Disruptions to shipping in the waterway due to the US-Israeli war with Iran have boosted global energy prices and inflation.
Maritime officials said on Wednesday that a container ship and a dry bulk carrier sank near the strait after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents.
Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past two weeks, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month.

Bolivia’s Energy Crisis Deepens as Natural Gas Reserves Run Dry
Bolivia's dwindling natural gas reserves and declining exports have undermined its economy and intensified fuel shortages.
Rising global energy prices and subsidy cuts have increased living costs and fueled widespread protests.
A $1.9 billion IMF rescue package and energy-sector reforms aim to stabilize the economy, but long-term recovery requires diversification.
Years of underinvestment in Bolivia’s gas industry have left the South American country facing a severe fuel shortage, as energy prices rise ever higher owing to the ongoing war in Iran. The energy shortages and economic crisis follow years of poor decision-making by the government.
In 2006, then-president Evo Morales took control of Bolivia’s fossil fuel industry, renegotiating contracts with international oil and gas companies and benefiting from the revenue. Much of the country’s newfound wealth was invested in public spending programmes, expensive fuel subsidies, and the maintenance of a fixed currency exchange rate pegged to the U.S. dollar. Fossil fuel revenues contributed heavily to Bolivia’s economy for several years, supporting GDP expansion and the development of social programmes that helped halve poverty rates .
For many years, Bolivian’s were led to believe that they had more extensive gas supplies than they actually did. However, in recent years, Bolivia’s fossil fuel sector has suffered as reserves have dwindled and no successful gas discoveries have occurred. As of April, Bolivia has an estimated 3.7 trillion cubic feet of proven reserves. The fall in gas production led exports to fall by almost 60 per cent over the last decade. Bolivia continues to rely heavily on natural gas , which accounts for around 70 per cent of its electricity mix.
Meanwhile, little progress has been made in developing the country’s green energy sector, leaving it facing severe energy shortages. The fall in gas revenues has left the economy suffering terribly, as inflation soars and the price of imported goods becomes ever more unaffordable. Luis Fernando Romero, the former head of an association of economists in southern Bolivia, stated, “We failed to take advantage of a historic opportunity that brought in immense revenue.”
This situation is not uncommon, with many other oil-rich states having had similar experiences. Several Middle Eastern states have long depended on oil and gas revenues for economic growth, and most have only recently announced plans to diversify their economies to reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Several countries across the MENA region announced new economic strategies following greater talk of a global green transition, which could leave them missing out on vital oil revenues if they don’t take moves to diversify and invest in value-added sectors.
The lack of investment in Bolivia’s other domestic sectors has left it struggling to stay afloat as it runs out of fuel and is forced to pay high fuel import costs. President Rodrigo Paz warned that “International prices are forcing us to make complex choices.”
In September, Bolivia’s Congress approved a $1.9 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), even though the terms of the deal require the government to impose strict austerity measures that could fuel social unrest. The loan received approval from the IMF’s Executive Board on October 2, and the government will now be required to cut its fuel subsidies and significantly reduce public spending. It has already increased fuel prices and is expected to scrap further gasoline subsidies from the beginning of next year. The loan is expected to unlock up to $4 billion more in financing from the World Bank and other lenders.
However, there are major concerns that the new financial plan will significantly increase the cost of living for households already struggling. Last December, the government reduced fuel subsidies, leaving little support for the most vulnerable Bolivians. This led to widespread protests as people called for President Paz’s resignation . In February, there was further social unrest after the distribution of poor-quality gasoline ruined thousands of vehicles. Then, in June and July, several weeks of road blockades by protesters occurred.
Meanwhile, to tackle the ongoing fuel shortages, Bolivia’s government announced plans in September to triple the fund financing refined fuel purchases, following similar announcements by Peru and Ecuador. This is expected to help mitigate diesel shortages and rising prices. Both Peru and Ecuador have increased fuel subsidies in recent months and are focusing on increasing production at state oil refineries to alleviate the price pressure of expensive fuel imports.
In July, Bolivia's Energy Minister Marcelo Blanco announced that the government had authorised the private sector to import and sell refined fuels to mitigate severe shortages. Then, in September, the government said that the state hydrocarbons firm plans to focus on exploration, extraction, and refining to continue developing Bolivia’s gas resources. However, experts warn that Bolivia could become a net fossil gas importer by around 2030 .
As Bolivia continues to battle fuel shortages and seeks to support economic recovery by borrowing from international organisations, the government must focus on diversifying the economy by developing other value-added sectors to sustain long-term growth. In addition, the government must also develop Bolivia’s renewable energy sources to reduce dependence on expensive fuel imports and ensure the country’s energy security.

items.title: Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas? - Al Jazeera

items.content:
Share Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas? on social media
Photo provided by the French Army shows a French army NH90 helicopter over the oil tanker Tagor, which is under international sanctions and was travelling from Russia in the Atlantic Sea, on Sunday, May 31, 2026 [File: French Army via AP]
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order waiving newly-passed Russia sanctions, claiming the move is in the US’s “national interest”.
Earlier this month, Trump also announced a deal to bring stocks of Russian diesel into global markets, in a bid to drive down energy prices that have spiked during the US-Israel war on Iran. The US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027.
Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered Ukraine, European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against its neighbour.
Ukraine’s President Volodmyr Zelenskyy slammed Trump’s diesel deal as “a gift” to Russia’s President Vladimir Putin that will help fund his war effort.
While European countries have also criticised Trump’s embrace of Russian energy, the US president has accused them of “hypocrisy”, as figures show that European Union countries continue to import Russian gas.
In his executive order on Friday, Trump called off numerous planned Russia-related sanctions days before they were due to take effect, including duties on Russian goods and penalties for buying the country’s oil and gas.
The now-blocked measures were part of legislation passed in Congress with bipartisan support last month , named after the late US Senator Lindsay Graham, an outspoken critic of Russia.
They would have included up to 100 percent tariffs on all goods brought into the US from the five top importers of Russian crude oil or gas, including China and India. They could also have imposed equal penalties on countries deemed to have knowingly bought oil or gas from Russia 30 days after the law’s implementation, or to be among the top five countries helping Moscow circumvent sanctions on sales of its oil.
The waiver will hold until the Trump administration believes “further action is appropriate”, according to the executive order.
US Congressman Don Beyer, a Democrat from Virginia, said the sanctions waiver amounts to a “surrender to Putin” that “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent”.
Vasily Astrov, an economist at the Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Russian government will likely be the greatest beneficiary because the easing of sanctions means Russian oil will not have to be further discounted.
He estimated that about 60 cents of every extra dollar in the price of a barrel of Russian oil would “end up in state coffers”.
Russian official Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Putin, hailed the US decision to waive the sanctions as “an important and truly historic moment”.
Other beneficiaries include major importers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India, who are now less exposed to the risk of secondary US penalties.
While Trump hopes the measures will also help bring down oil prices for US consumers before November mid-term elections, experts say that is less certain.
Addressing the US’s recent diesel deal with Russia, EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said it is unlikely to have a significant impact on global prices.
According to Trump, that deal would bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel into US and global markets “immediately”, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November, and 1 million tonnes afterwards.
“If we look at the volumes, they are not of any macroeconomic significance, and frankly, there are strong doubts whether Russia is even able to supply those volumes, and according also to US quality standards, those are big question marks,” Dombrovskis told the AFP news agency.
China and India are the largest buyers of Russian crude oil, purchasing 6 billion euros ($6.74bn) and 3.6 billion euros ($4.04bn) worth respectively in September, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a nonprofit think tank.
Hungary and Slovakia, the landlocked EU members that have exemptions to the bloc’s ban on Russian crude, also remain big customers, buying a combined 290 million euros ($326m) worth of the commodity in September, said CREA. Turkiye imported 172 million euros ($193m) worth of Russian crude oil the same month, the think tank added.
Since the end of 2022, the largest importers of Russian oil products, which include diesel, have been Turkiye, China, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Singapore.
Saudi Arabia imported the most Russian oil products in September at 534 million euros ($600m), followed by Turkiye with 321 million euros ($361m), China with 304 million euros ($342m) and India with 161 million euros ($181m).
Is Europe buying increasing amounts of gas from Russia?
“The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” European leaders said in a joint statement adopted following a two-day European Council meeting in Brussels this week.
But despite its own near-blanket ban on Russian oil, the EU has continued to import large quantities of Russian gas, though it plans to phase out those imports next year .
Urgewald, a Germany-based group that researches coal companies, reported this week that more than 12 million tonnes of Russian Arctic LNG was transported into EU ports from January to September this year, a 9.5 percent jump from the same period last year.
In September, EU countries imported 817 million euros ($918m) of pipeline gas, and 615 million euros ($691m) of liquefied natural gas (LNG), according to CREA.
EU members France and the Netherlands were the largest LNG importers, bringing in 446 million euros ($501m) and 116 million euros ($130m) respectively, according to the think tank. France’s LNG imports represented a 103 percent increase from the previous month, it added.
France’s President Emmanuel Macron has been among the most outspoken about Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, saying on Friday that it “sends a negative message” and would have no impact on global prices.
Hungary imported the most Russian pipeline gas of any EU member by far during the month, with 414 million euros ($465m) worth. Slovakia and Bulgaria brought in 161 million euros ($181m) and 132 million euros ($148m), respectively, according to CREA data.

Ukraine war briefing: Russia building non-negotiable ‘security zone’ inside Ukrainian border, Putin declares
Russian president says area will not be part of any potential peace talks while Kremlin says the zone spans 660km. What we know on day 1,697
Russia is establishing a “security zone” inside Ukraine along the border and it will be non-negotiable in any ⁠future talks with Kyiv, Vladimir Putin has said . The Russian president, wearing military uniform and speaking during a visit to a command post, said the operation ⁠was in response to Ukraine’s ⁠2024-25 incursion into ​Russia’s western Kursk region . “The Russian armed forces were tasked not only with expelling the enemy from our land but also with establishing a security zone ⁠in the adjacent territory. This task is being carried out successfully,” he said in televised comments on Friday. “Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions ⁠for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with ​Ukraine.”
The planned ‌security zone spanned 660km (410 ‌miles) , of which 70% was currently under Russia’s control, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said. Peskov did not say how deep it would ‌reach inside Ukraine. The zone requires Russia to carve out land in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, which are not among those it is illegally claiming as its own territory.
Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling the US Congress the pause on the legislation which passed both chambers was in the national interest. The US president said in an executive order on Friday he was waiving many ⁠sanctions, restrictions and duties ⁠on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticising ⁠Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service had not yet been fully restored , as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House. Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels and asked the EU for another €70bn ($79bn/£59bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia, report Jennifer Rankin and Andrew Roth . Hours earlier Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” after his purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
A Russian ⁠airstrike on ​Kherson in southern ⁠Ukraine killed one ⁠person ​and ‌injured ‌19 others , the governor ‌said on Saturday. The person ‌killed was an ​ambulance driver and ⁠a child ​was among the ​injured, ​Oleksandr Prokudin ​said ‌on ​Telegram.
Russian attacks on Friday killed at least eight people and injured 60 ⁠across Ukraine, hit two shopping centres and cut power to more than 1 million people after strikes on the energy grid, ⁠officials said. Two were kiled and 12 more wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, governor Oleh Syniehubov ⁠said. Further Russian strikes through the evening injured nine, officials said. Attacks in Kramatorsk in the eastern Donetsk region killed two and another two were killed in south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.
A drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight in the north-western region of Volyn , according to governor Roman Romaniuk, leaving 370,000 people temporarily without power. Drone attacks also struck a customs terminal ​and torched about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, he said. Other attacks hit at least two shopping centres – one in the northern city of Sumy and another in the neighbouring region of ⁠Rivne, officials said.
The attacks came as a new report showed that civilian casualties from Russia’s invasion have climbed steeply. At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded last month – a total that is 85% higher than in September last year, the report from the UN human rights office in Kyiv said on Friday. It said intensifying Russian attacks in October already had killed dozens of civilians, including children. “The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, the UN office head.
As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian, writes Andrew Roth in this analysis .

items.title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
items.summary: Defence Minister Guido Crosetto tells the BBC the US risks prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to end it.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Europe preparing for 'possibility of madness' from Russia, says Italy's defence minister
By Sarah Rainsford Eastern and Southern Europe correspondent ,Â  Reporting from Rome
Italy's defence minister has said it was a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.
Guido Crosetto warned in a BBC interview that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace. Trump has denied asking for satellite access to be suspended.
Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice" and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.
Trump agreed the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.
Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.
Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.
"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side â and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness â then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.
Image caption, Italy's prime minister has become a close ally of Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky
Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.
The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.
Crosetto said that victory for Ukraine would be "a victory for peace, a victory for justice, a victory for international law".
He vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting Italy's parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.
The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.
That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.
At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".
Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".
But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.
"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.
Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'
Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.
During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms instead of education.
Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."
In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.
Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the IxÃ¨ institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.
There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.
But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow â targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".
"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.
"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."
Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.
The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".
A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.
But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.
"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.

CENTCOM says 'vast majority' of Iran's attempted attacks on Strait of Hormuz are 'unsuccessful'
U.S. Central Command Spokesperson U.S. Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins speaks to Fox News Digital about Operation Epic Fury against Iran.
The "vast majority" of Iran's attempted attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz are "unsuccessful" as the key waterway remains open for transit, U.S. Central Command Spokesperson U.S. Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins told Fox News Digital this week.
Hawkins spoke after CENTCOM said the GFS Pride, a Singapore-flagged, Cyprus-owned container ship was hit by an Iranian projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday and sunk while being towed ashore due to a fire on board the ship.
"The vast majority of Iran's attempted attacks on innocent civilian mariners transiting an international waterway, being the Strait of Hormuz, they are unsuccessful. As a matter of fact, the U.S. military has assisted in providing coordinated protection for thousands of ships that have safely transited," Hawkins said. "That translates to about 97% of the ships that have sought to transit the Strait of Hormuz have done so successfully without being hit by an Iranian projectile.
"But let's be clear here, what the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran is doing is unjustified and it's also unsuccessful because they are not achieving their objective of closing the Strait of Hormuz," he added. "It is open, it is available for transit, and we've seen that transit continue this very day."
LIVE UPDATES: IRANIAN ARMY SPOKESPERSON SAYS STRAIT OF HORMUZ WILL REOPEN 'IF AMERICA LEAVES THE REGION'
An MH-60R Sea Hawk helicopter lands on the flight deck of USS Rafael Peralta as it transits regional waters, in this photo released by U.S. Central Command on Oct. 15, 2026. CENTCOM said the USS Rafael Peralta is enforcing a military blockade of Iranian ports. (CENTCOM)
In an update Friday from CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper, he said, "In recent days and months, we have seen the IRGC continually attack merchant ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, and in many cases kill innocent civilian mariners.
"The International Maritime Organization reports that more than 20 civilian mariners have been killed by Iran's attacks against commercial shipping since February," Cooper continued.
"Over the last seven days alone, about 400 merchant ships have sailed through the Strait. U.S. forces have also assisted Gulf partners in shipping over 100 million barrels of crude oil during the same period, adding to the more than 1.3 billion barrels of crude we have helped regional allies ship through the Strait in recent months," he added.
Hawkins also told Fox News Digital that he thinks "every American should be proud of American service members who are serving across the Middle East, in particular focusing on doing two things at once as it relates to Iran.
VIDEO: ISRAEL'S AMBASSADOR TO THE UN ISSUES STARK WARNING TO IRAN, HEZBOLLAH DURING ELECTION PERIOD
Vessels are seen in the Strait of Hormuz near Musandam, Oman, on Oct. 2, 2026. (Reuters)
"And one is helping maintain flow through the Strait of Hormuz in the form of commercial vessels despite Iran's unjustified aggression," Hawkins said, noting that thousands of ships have crossed through the waterway over the last few months, "in addition to more than 1 billion barrels of crude oil.
"At the same time that they are encouraging traffic flow in support of international shipping, they are maintaining a steel wall blockade against Iran. There have been no exports or imports to Iran without U.S. permission in the form of allowing humanitarian ships to go through," Hawkins continued. "So that shows the precision, dedication, and professionalism of our troops who are executing this complex mission — not just one — but two at the same time."
More than 50,000 U.S. service members are currently stationed across the Middle East, according to Hawkins.
A U.S. Air Force F-15E Strike Eagle is refueled by a KC-135 Stratotanker while patrolling the skies over the Middle East, according to CENTCOM, in this image released on Oct. 2, 2026. (CENTCOM)
"They are highly vigilant, they are highly dedicated, and they're serving with courage and bravery. And they're doing so alongside our regional allies and partners. It shouldn't be forgotten that we continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf allies and partners to help them defend their airspace from unjustified and unwarranted attacks from Iran, and we have been highly successful in working together, and will continue to do that," he said.

items.title: TSMC Says AI Chip Demand Is Still Far Above What It Can Supply. That's Why I'd Buy Nvidia Stock. - Yahoo Finance
items.summary: TSMC Says AI Chip Demand Is Still Far Above What It Can Supply. That's Why I'd Buy Nvidia Stock.  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
TSMC Says AI Chip Demand Is Still Far Above What It Can Supply. That's Why I'd Buy Nvidia Stock.
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) investors got a new look at the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) chips on Thursday, Oct. 15. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM), which makes chip wafers for Nvidia, posted third-quarter revenue of $46.7 billion -- over the high end of the $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion range management had forecast in July.
And TSMC's chairman and CEO, C.C. Wei, didn't sound worried about what's next.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
"[T]he demand actually is still far above our capability today to supply," Wei said on the company's earnings call. He made the comment in an answer where he wouldn't say if that demand comes more from AI accelerators or central processing units (CPUs).
Nvidia stock, though, headed the other way. Shares ended Thursday at $217.23, off around 9% from the record close they set on Oct. 6 ($239.24).
I think the gap between what Nvidia's supplier is reporting and what Nvidia's stock is doing makes the shares worth buying now.
Showing how much AI is powering the chipmaker, TSMC's revenue from high-performance computing (the platform that includes AI chips) climbed 22% sequentially in the third quarter. That was faster than the platform's 20% sequential growth in the second quarter. High-performance computing is now 68% of TSMC's revenue, up from 57% in the third quarter of 2025. Overall, TSMC's revenue grew 41% year over year in U.S. dollars. Net income , which TSMC reports in New Taiwan dollars, rose 69%.
Management expects more. TSMC guided for fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. The midpoint is around 14% over the third quarter's total, so the company is calling for another double-digit sequential gain after a 16% climb in the third quarter.
TSMC now sees 2026 revenue growing about 44% in U.S. dollars, up from its July outlook of a little over 40%.
Wei also pushed back on any idea that AI chip demand is cooling. He was asked about TSMC's forecast that its AI accelerator revenue would rise at an average yearly rate in the mid- to high-50% range from 2024 to 2029. Wei said "we did not see any sign of slowdown," adding that the rate "probably will be higher."
TSMC doesn't say how much of its revenue comes from Nvidia. So its report isn't a direct preview of Nvidia's next quarter.
But Nvidia sells chips on both sides of the split Wei wouldn't talk about. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) remain its main business, and last quarter it announced Vera, a CPU made for AI agents.
TSMC's fourth-quarter outlook covers October to December. And because chips take months to move from TSMC's wafers to finished Nvidia products, that forecast arguably says more about Nvidia's next few quarters than about the one ending this month.
And Nvidia's own results point the same way as TSMC's. Revenue rose to $96.2 billion in the second quarter of its fiscal 2027 (which ended July 26, 2026), up 18% from fiscal Q1 and 106% year over year. Management forecast around $108 billion in fiscal Q3, plus or minus 2%.
Of course, a shortage doesn't last forever. TSMC spent around $40.6 billion on capital expenditures through the first three quarters of 2026, and when supply eventually catches up to demand, Nvidia might lose some of its pricing power. But that doesn't look like a problem for the next few quarters.
At around $217, Nvidia's share price is about 14 times the earnings per share analysts expect for its next fiscal year (ending January 2028), on average. At the Oct. 6 record, it was around 15 times expected earnings. TSMC's shares, by comparison, go for about 19 times earnings, based on analysts' average forecast for 2027.
Put another way, investors are paying less for every dollar of Nvidia's expected profit than for TSMC's, even though Nvidia's revenue climbed more than twice as fast in each company's latest quarter. The market seems to doubt that Nvidia's growth can last.
Sure, that doubt might be right. If AI spending slows, Nvidia's sales could drop faster than those of a foundry with many kinds of customers. But TSMC's report doesn't show any sign of that yet.
In the end, I'd consider buying Nvidia stock at this price. I'd just keep the stake small. The stock is risky and volatile. After all, the shares dropped 9% in just seven trading days this month.
The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Nvidia wasn't one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.
Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $391,581 !* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $1,334,780 !*
Now, it's worth noting Stock Advisor's total average return is 936% — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 213% for the S&P 500. Don't miss the latest top 10 list, available with Stock Advisor , and join an investing community built by individual investors for individual investors.

items.content:
Fighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a rally to recruit more fighters in Sana’a. Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images
Fighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a rally to recruit more fighters in Sana’a. Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images
UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains
United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers
Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?
The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.
The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible sign that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.
Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.
Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations inside Yemen in January, cutting off its funding supply line.
Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.
Yemeni Southern Giants Brigades fighters celebrate and wave their weapons. Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.
Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.
There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.
The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen , and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.
Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough
UAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, the Houthis are determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.
On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.
The missiles landed about 500 metres from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 metres from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.
The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.
Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.
In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging more closely with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.
The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.
Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.
No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.

items.content:
Wijdan Abu Matar, front, has managed to bring her children together in Cairo, Egypt, but her husband, Hatem, remains in Gaza. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian
Wijdan Abu Matar, front, has managed to bring her children together in Cairo, Egypt, but her husband, Hatem, remains in Gaza. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian
‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in Gaza
Families have been scattered, fathers separated from their children, and couples unable to reunite and marry
Wijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leave Gaza in November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment, while her injured husband, Hatem, remained behind.
Wijdan and her family were living in the Nuseirat refugee camp when the Gaza war began with the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Ten days later, on 17 October that year, an Israeli strike hit the al-Muhandseen tower, near their home, injuring Wijdan and every member of her family.
“We were sitting together, just about to start lunch when the bombing happened,” Wijdan recalled. “The ceiling collapsed over our heads. Everything went dark. I couldn’t see anything. I just started screaming the names of my sons and daughters.”
Her daughter Nour, 15, suffered the most serious injuries, including a fractured skull and bleeding in the brain. Five-year-old Amna suffered severe burns to her chest. The family was initially separated after the strike.
Nour spent about 33 days in intensive care, with Wijdan by her side. Amna and Aysel, three and a half, were at a different hospital for 15 days.
Aysel, who incurred severe burns in the bombing, holds up a photograph of her father. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian On 30 November 2023, Wijdan travelled with Nour to a hospital in Egypt for treatment. For months, the family remained scattered across Egypt, receiving medical treatment and staying with other relatives.
“I felt completely helpless,” Wijdan said. “There was a fire in my heart because I was away from my husband and my family was scattered.”
Eventually, Wijdan managed to bring her children together in an apartment in Egypt. Three years on, however, she is still separated from her husband, who remains in Gaza. “I have become both the mother and the father to my children,” she said. “The responsibility is exhausting me, and I am constantly worried about my husband.”
Hatem suffered a serious leg injury that limits his mobility and is now displaced in a tent in Nuseirat. Even speaking to him is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection. “When he manages to get online, he calls me and the children. He tells me, ‘I am counting the days until I can see you again.’ I can see the tears in his eyes,” Wijdan says.
Speaking to Hatem is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection, Wijdan says. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian Wijdan has no regular source of income and relies on donations. Hatem stopped receiving a salary 10 months ago and his injury prevents him from working.
In Egypt, life is difficult for Wijdan and her family. She says she cannot afford transportation to send five of her children to school. “I see my children’s future slipping away in front of me, and there is nothing I can do.”
Nour still requires medical treatment, but Wijdan often cannot afford her medication. She sometimes considers returning to Gaza to be with Hatem, but fears exposing her children to further suffering.
“I dream of getting my children the treatment they need, and I hope we can reunite with my husband as soon as possible so he can also receive treatment,” Wijdan said. “I cannot carry all of this alone. Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war.”
‘Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war,’ says Wijdan Abu Matar. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian Since the war began with Hamas’s attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry. Earlier this year an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continues to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks
Sami Abu Tabaq, a 29-year-old Palestinian photojournalist, was forced to leave the Gaza Strip in April 2024, leaving behind his family and his fiancee, Ola.
“Loneliness kills me every day,” he said. “Life away from the woman I love and my family is incredibly hard. I’m desperately waiting for the day God brings us together again.”
Sami became engaged to Ola five months before the war began. They had met by chance when he chose her family’s home as a location for a photoshoot. Before the war, they saw each other constantly. They went to the sea, had dinner at restaurants in Gaza, and spent months preparing the house where they planned to live after their wedding, which was scheduled for November 2023.
Sami and his family fled their home in Tal al-Zaatar, Jabaliya, early on in the war. Their home was badly damaged and later destroyed, along with the house Sami and Ola had been planning to move into once they got married.
When his sister decided to flee south with her children, Sami accompanied her but he could not reach Ola to say goodbye.
The separation became unbearable. Days, sometimes weeks, passed without Sami knowing whether Ola was alive. Once, he saw reports that an entire residential block near her home in Gaza City had been bombed. “I almost lost my mind. I had never felt so helpless,” he said. Unable to return north, he asked his brother to check on her. Eventually, his brother confirmed that she and her family were alive.
‘I couldn’t cry over my children like everyone else’: the tragedy of Palestinian journalist Wael al-Dahdouh
Sami continued working as a photojournalist from southern Gaza. Four journalists who had shared his tent were later killed, including Hamza al-Dahdouh, a son of the Al Jazeera journalist Wael al-Dahdouh.
As Israel threatened a ground invasion of Rafah in 2024, Ola began urging Sami to leave Gaza, fearing he would be killed. Sami paid a company coordinating exits at the time for both of them to cross into Egypt. But Ola could not reach southern Gaza to travel through Rafah. “She told me, ‘You go, and I’ll follow you,’” Sami said. “And here we are, still waiting, nearly two and a half years later.” They still have not managed to get married.
By his second day in Egypt, Sami was overwhelmed by guilt. “The overthinking kills me,” he said. “I felt ashamed to turn on the lights or eat proper food while my fiancee and my family were struggling to find the most basic things.”
In Egypt, his life has become dominated by loneliness and sleeplessness. “There is safety in Egypt and there are beautiful places, but I stay home. Happiness has no meaning without her. I cannot enjoy anything while she is not here,” he said.
Sami Abu Tabaq sits alone in his apartment in Cairo, while his fiancee, Ola, remains in Gaza. Images of Gaza are shown on the television. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian Despite the war, Ola completed her bachelor’s degree in nursing at the Islamic University of Gaza. She has also endured enormous loss: her cousin, the journalist Ayat Khadoura , was killed, along with about 50 other members of her extended family.
From Egypt, Sami tries to create moments of happiness for her. For her latest birthday, he contacted her brother in Gaza and secretly arranged a cake, gift and flowers. “When she woke up and saw everything, she was so happy. I love her reaction when she’s happy.” The only problem was the flowers. “They were artificial,” he said. “I wasn’t happy with them, but natural flowers can’t get into Gaza because Israel does not allow them in.”
Sami says he has tried every possible way to get Ola out, without success. She is now applying for scholarships abroad, hoping education might provide a route to evacuation and, eventually, to him.
Sami recently travelled to Mecca for Umrah, where one prayer remained constantly on his mind. “I prayed, ‘God, please bring us together soon,’” he said. “But one thing I know for sure: I will wait for her for the rest of my life, until God brings us together.”

items.title: Actress Selma Blair says she 'did not intend to harm anyone' in plane altercation
items.summary: A publicist for the actress said the incident stemmed from a "medical emergency" and said she has a neurological disorder that can cause out-of-control responses.
items.content:
US actress Selma Blair has spoken out after being accused of assaulting multiple people on a flight to New York.
A publicist for the Legally Blonde star said she "did not intend to harm anyone" and that there was "much more to this story". Blair "experienced a medical emergency on the flight" and is still fighting âmultiple sclerosis (MS), a statement read.
Blair's publicist said that the 54-year-old had a neurological disorder that "bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her".
The star pleaded not guilty to charges that she assaulted an officer and a nurse after being removed from the flight. She was also accused of assaulting two flight attendants on board.
Blair's team said the public account of what happened to her aboard a Delta Airlines flight to New York had been "built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline".
They also denied media reports that she had attempted to open the door of the aircraft.
The publicist noted Blair's fight against multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic illness the actress revealed publicly in 2018. She announced in 2021 that she was in remission for the disease, but the statement noted that the Hellboy and Cruel Intentions star "still has bad days".
It added that she also has pseudobulbar affect (PBA) - a disorder that develops in the context of a brain injury or underlying neurological dysfunction, according to the US National Institutes of Health.
The disorder affects emotional expression that can result in sudden involuntary and out-of-control episodes of laughing, crying or anger that do not match how a person actually feels.
Figure caption, Watch: Selma Blair is seen leaving court after plane incident
Blair's publicist described the actress's physical achievements since her MS diagnosis as "nothing short of a miracle" and said she still lives with pain daily.
"Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night," she said. "There is much more to this story than has been reported and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgement, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion."
The incident happened on a flight travelling from Los Angeles to New York on Sunday evening. New York airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on a Delta Airlines flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.
A pilot asked for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to audio recorded on air traffic control obtained by CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
Blair was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons by the FBI for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US that relates to the on-board altercation.
The two additional charges of assault were filed in state court after she was taken off the plane. She has pleaded not guilty to those charges and was released on bail.

items.title: Berkshire shares buck market sell-off, rally to highest since Buffett said he would step down as CEO
items.summary: Berkshire Hathaway shares are at their highest level since Warren Buffett told shareholders at the May 2025 annual meeting he planned to step down as CEO at the end of that year.
items.content:
Berkshire rally to highest since Buffett announcement
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire Hathaway shares closed Friday at their highest level since Warren Buffett told shareholders at the May 2025 annual meeting he planned to step down as CEO at the end of that year .
The day before that Saturday surprise, both the  Class A and Class B shares had closed at all-time highs.
Over the next three months, they lost more than 14% of their value as investors worried a " Buffett premium " was dissolving.
It's been more than a year since their post-meeting low in August of 2025, and the recovery has not been a straight line, but BRK.A ended Friday at $798,000, just 1.4% below its all-time closing high of $809,350.
The B shares finished at $532.02, also 1.4% under their all-time closing high of $539.80.
A loss Thursday broke a 10-session winning streak that added 5% to Berkshire's stock prices but they rebounded with gains of more than 1% Friday.
CNBC Pro thinks investors may be happy Berkshire is spending some of its big cash pile under CEO Greg Abel, with  $4.5 billion of buybacks in Q2 , investments in  Alphabet , Taylor Morrison Home , Lennar , (although there haven't been any buys of that stock since October 2), and now, Bending Spoons . (More on that below).
It also notes Keefe, Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields believes higher short-term interest rates are helping to lift the shares.
Berkshire still has roughly $360 billion in cash, "a good symbol of continued patience under the new CEO," and those higher rates mean "they'll be making more money" on that money.
In addition, its insurance operations have benefited from a quiet hurricane season so far.
Higher oil prices are good for its $19 billion stake in  Chevron , which closed Friday at an all-time high after gaining almost 36% since the start of July. Berkshire's energy-related  subsidiaries are also getting a tailwind.
And recently, Berkshire may be getting a boost as investors  shift away from high-flying AI and tech stocks and turn to "old" economy names .
For example, Coca-Cola , a long-time Buffett favorite and now a $37.6 billion holding , also closed Friday at an all-time high, perhaps with some extra help from KFC's switch from Pepsi to Coke . It's up 34% year-to-date.
Berkshire's position has gained $2.4 billion since last Friday, overtaking Alphabet to become the third largest stake in its portfolio. (See the full top 10 below.)
Berkshire's B shares have cut their June 1 deficit of 17.5 percentage points versus the  S&P 500 by almost two-thirds.
They are now 6.0 percentage points behind the benchmark for the year.
Atypical bet on 'buzzy' Italian tech company is big win ... so far
Berkshire Hathaway's surprising bet of close to $1 billion on  Bending Spoons is paying off big, at least in the short term.
The Italian company, which began trading on Nasdaq in the U.S. in July, buys cast-off internet names like AOL, Evernote, and Vimeo, uses AI to cut costs, and deploys the savings to make more acquisitions.
In late July, CNBC Pro said , "Wall Street is buzzing," and "analysts ... see big gains ahead."
The tech stock is decidedly not a typical Berkshire  value play , trading at a large multiple to its earnings.
Matteo Danieli, co-founder of Bending Spoons, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Wednesday, July 1, 2026.
But before Wall Street's open Wednesday morning, a Bending Spoons  news release revealed Berkshire is investing a "further" $330 million in the company by purchasing 10 million newly issued shares at $33 per share in a private placement .
That was already an almost 12% discount from Tuesday's closing price of $37.86 and the news sent Bending Spoons shares even higher .
They hit an intraday high of $58.56 before closing up 41% at $53.46 on Wednesday.
Bending Spoons shares are up 24.3% over the three trading days since the revelation, after giving up a chunk of their earlier gains in  Friday's tech sell-off to end at $47.07.
That's a solid 42.6% higher than Berkshire's $33 purchase price for a profit, on paper, of nearly $141 million.
But what's that "further" in Bending Spoon's statement?
The release also disclosed, apparently for the first time, that Berkshire invested $600 million at Bending Spoon's IPO more than three months ago.
The release doesn't specify how many shares Berkshire bought in July, and Bending Spoons wouldn't confirm my math, but assuming Berkshire paid the $29 per share IPO price, that initial purchase would have been almost 20.7 million shares.
That puts Berkshire's holding now at close to 30.7 million shares, which would be worth more than $1.4 billion at Friday's close, a gain of 55.3% for its overall investment of $930 million.
Bending Spoons shares soar after Berkshire reveals $330M investment, taking a 4% stake
Bending Spoon's release also says the "new investment brings Berkshire Hathaway's ownership to 4%."
The company told me in an email it hasn't "specifically disclosed" how many outstanding shares it has now, "but we had 635 million fully diluted weighted average shares outstanding in Q2, we issued 34 million shares as part of the IPO, and we will be issuing an additional 10 million as part of this transaction."
Using those numbers, Berkshire's presumed 30.7 million shares are a 4.5% stake, and that's what I've put in the  Berkshire Portfolio Tracker for now.
We may learn more next month about exactly how many shares Berkshire bought in the IPO when its portfolio snapshot as of September 30 is due to be disclosed.
Another unknown: who at Berkshire made the call to take a stake in Bending Spoons.
Bending Spoons CEO Luca Ferrari: We'll buy any company as long as we think we can make it better
Bending Spoons CEO and Co-Founder Luca Ferrari shares Wall Street's enthusiasm about Berkshire's investments, saying in the news release the Omaha company "has been among the finest and most respected capital allocators in the world, and is a longstanding inspiration for Bending Spoons."
Morningstar's Greggory Warren (who was one of the designated analyst questioners at Berkshire shareholders meetings from 2014 to 2019 ) writes the Bending Spoons buy, along with Berkshire's now $36 billion stake in  Alphabet , show "the firm is finally moving out of its comfort zone to find places to put capital to work, which should be viewed as a positive for long-term investors."
At Barron's , Andrew Bary says , "Many Berkshire holders would like to see the company invest more heavily in stocks given the company's $350 billion-plus in cash, but Bending Spoons was a surprise" given its high valuation.

The Motley Fool on Yahoo Finance: Berkshire Hathaway Outperformed the S&P 500 Over a 60-Year Period Under Warren Buffett. Here's the Stock That Could Help Continue the Streak Under Greg Abel.
Warren Buffett defends Coca-Cola , a big and long-time Berkshire Hathaway holding, against health concerns over sugary beverages.
WARREN BUFFETT : Yeah well — people have been drinking Coca-Cola since 1886, so I imagine that there's been some —
I don't know of any study that's been made on the lifetime of heavy users of Coca-Cola versus people who drink nothing but water.
But speaking for myself, I'm 84, literally one-quarter of all the calories I've consumed in the last 30 years have been Coca-Cola. And I don't see how anybody can feel any better than I feel.
I am one-quarter Coca-Cola, and I can tell you, I haven't missed a day of work, you know — since I had the prostate cancer — radiation — three years ago. And I don't think the prostate cancer was caused (laughs) by Coca-Cola.
So there's 1.9 billion eight-ounce servings of Coca-Cola products sold around the world today, and there will be more than 1.9 billion a year from now, and more than that five years from now, and more than that ten years from now.
And that's been true.  And some people will like other things, and — and if they like broccoli and Brussels sprouts, God bless them, you know, but don't invite me for dinner.  (Laughter)

items.summary: US, Israel face threats of war if oil prices keep rising  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
Oil prices over $100 could affect war with Iran, leading to escalation before elections - analysis
The US and Israel know that the main hurdle to keeping the lid on the war with Iran is the price of oil, and it will keep rising if no solution can be found for Hormuz and the Houthis.
Vessels transit the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of the port city of Bandar Abbas in southern Iran on September 5, 2026; illustrative
( photo credit : ATTA KENARE / AFP via Getty Images )
High oil prices are going to be an issue over the next few weeks if they continue to stay above $100 a barrel. That is a clear challenge for the United States and also potentially for Israel in terms of keeping a lid on a renewed conflict with Iran prior to the elections in both countries.
It is no secret that the looming elections have shifted dynamics, expectations, and assessments of whether the conflict could restart.
The high oil prices come amid a decline in stock prices on Wall Street, amid concerns about AI companies and energy prices. That could tend to be a kind of triple threat affecting the United States, and thus also affecting Israel.
That is because the United States has been working hard to keep diesel and oil prices from skyrocketing. There has been a lot of messaging that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that other energy sources exist, but the question is whether the global market will accept those assertions.
Recent videos showing ships sinking in the Strait of Hormuz and all sorts of containers floating away as ships are in distress are certainly not something that will boost global optimism regarding supply chains, and it always remains a question whether enough ships are transporting energy supplies.
Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on October 3, 2026. (credit: AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES)
It also leads to questions about what the Houthis might do. The Houthis could try to threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They could also encourage other Iranian proxies, such as those in Iraq, to continue attacks on Saudi oil and gas energy infrastructure.
A mysterious explosion in Iraq on Saturday appears to have struck an Iranian proxy group there. All this could continue to disrupt global trade. For example, when attacks hit pipelines or transit points in Saudi Arabia, repairs can take weeks. That creates disruption, and all those disruptions add up to the feeling in the global market that there is too much uncertainty.
This kind of uncertainty will affect the US. It already appears to be affecting policy regarding the Ukraine-Russia war, and this is the kind of thing that can lead to escalation in the Middle East or miscalculations in which something happens again with Iran.
Meanwhile, Iran continues to be blockaded , but it also tends to feel a bit confident about its next steps. As a result, we see potential for escalation within the next week or two.
Iran also knows there are elections in Israel and the United States; therefore, Iran and its proxies may want to take advantage of this period.

items.content:
Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the 1st time since 2023
Trump criticized the moving, calling on the Fed to "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES."
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Wednesday in an effort to battle back a monthslong surge of inflation set off by the Iran war . The move marks the central bank's first rate increase since July 2023.
The central bank hiked its benchmark rate a quarter of a percentage point, putting interest rates at a level between 3.75% and 4%.
Hours after the announcement, President Donald Trump criticized the move, repeating a call for lower interest rates that he has made on multiple occasions since his return to office last year.
The Federal Reserve Building is the headquarters of the Federal Reserve System and 12 Federal Reserve Banks, in Washington, D.C.
"LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" Trump said in a social media post.
However later, Trump told ABC News that despite the Fed doing the opposite of what he has demanded he still has confidence in Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
"I’m relying on Kevin, but he’s got a very tough board," Trump said from the tarmac while traveling to a campaign rally in North Carolina, referring to the 12-member policymaking board. "He's got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high, they’re not appropriate."
Trump insisted the Fed raised rates “only for political reasons” and to hurt him.
“They’re raising the rates to make Trump do as bad as he can possibly do," he said. "The problem they have is that we have the greatest economy in history."
Earlier Wednesday, the board, including Trump-appointed Warsh, voted unanimously in favor of the rate increase.
That current level of interest rates marks a significant drop from a recent peak attained in 2023, but borrowing costs remain well above a 0% rate established at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Iran live updates: Sticker shock woes rise after Saudi refinery stops crude loading
The major stock indexes turned lower after the policy announcement. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 630 points, or 1.2%, while the S & P 500 dropped 0.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq ticked down 0.01%.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," Warsh said at a press conference in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. "The committee’s unanimous vote shows our resolve to achieve price stability on a timelier basis."
The move appears aimed at containing a recent bout of price increases. Global oil prices are hovering near a four-month high and the average price for a gallon of gasoline tops $4.30, according to AAA .
The U.S. economy has shown signs of additional strain in recent days, including a bond selloff that is pushing up borrowing costs for credit cards and mortgages.
The price woes previously divided central bankers eager to contain inflation but reluctant to cool off the economy and weaken the labor market.
The Fed opted to hold interest rates steady at its most recent meeting in July. Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board, however, voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction in a decade.

Warsh, who took the helm of the central bank in May, has vowed to cool off persistently elevated price increases.
"The Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices," Warsh said in remarks last month at the Fed's annual summer gathering in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference following Federal Open Market Committee meetings at Federal Reserve Headquarters, September 16, 2026 in Washington.
Prices rose 3.4% in August compared to a year earlier, maintaining the same level from the prior month, federal government data last week showed.
Inflation stands more than a percentage point higher than the Federal Reserve's target rate of 2%.
Despite a stubborn bout of inflation, the economy remains fairly robust by some measures.
A blockbuster jobs report earlier this month showed employers added 162,000 workers in August, demonstrating continued resilience for the nation's labor market. The economy grew over three months ending in June, defying fear of a downturn triggered by the Iran war.
Fighting in the Middle East kept global crude prices above $105 a barrel as of Wednesday, which amounted to a rise of about 50% since the Iran war broke out in late February.
Inflation holds steady at elevated level as Iran war pushes up gas prices
The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. stands at $4.36, putting it more than $1.30 higher than before the war, AAA data showed.
Record-high diesel prices have raised transport costs for many everyday products, including groceries, clothes and furniture.
The war in Iran, which began with a large-scale U.S.-Israeli attack in the winter, prompted Iran's near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which facilitates one-fifth of global crude supply. Saudi Arabia over the weekend shut down a key pipeline bypassing the strait, which further constrained oil delivery and put upward pressure on prices.
